statement: Air trapped in a syringe can be compressed because there are large gaps between its particles.
explanation: True! Pushing the plunger brings gas particles closer together; it does not make each particle smaller.

statement: A sealed balloon contains nothing because the air inside is invisible.
explanation: False! Air is matter: it has mass and occupies space even though we cannot see it.

statement: When air is compressed, each gas particle becomes smaller.
explanation: False! The spaces between particles decrease. The particles themselves do not shrink.

statement: Pouring water from a narrow cup into a wide bowl changes its shape, but not its volume if none is lost.
explanation: True! Liquid particles can slide past one another, so the liquid changes shape while keeping its volume.

statement: An ice cube keeps its shape because its particles do not move at all.
explanation: False! Particles in solid ice vibrate about fixed positions. A fixed shape does not mean no movement.

statement: Gas from a small container can spread throughout a larger empty container without adding more gas.
explanation: True! Gas particles move freely and spread out to fill the available volume. Their number need not increase.

statement: Air near a busy road must be clean if no smoke is visible.
explanation: False! Some harmful gases and very small particles cannot be seen. Clear-looking air is not proof that it is clean.

statement: To compare soot near a road and in a garden fairly, identical sticky traps should be left out for the same length of time.
explanation: True! Keeping trap size, coating and exposure time the same makes location the factor being compared.

statement: A full sealed bottle may crack in a freezer because water takes up more space when it freezes.
explanation: True! Water expands when it becomes ice, which can push against the bottle.

statement: Ice melting into water and salt dissolving in water are the same process.
explanation: False! Melting changes a solid into its liquid state. Dissolving mixes a substance into a solvent.

statement: Pure water must boil at 100°C everywhere, including on top of a high mountain.
explanation: False! Boiling point depends on pressure. Lower atmospheric pressure on a high mountain lets water boil below 100°C.

statement: While pure water boils at constant standard atmospheric pressure, adding heat can make more water change into gas without raising its temperature above its boiling point.
explanation: True! During boiling, the added energy supports the change of state rather than raising the temperature of the boiling water.

statement: Water particles disappear when liquid water becomes water vapour.
explanation: False! The water particles remain present in the gas state; they are farther apart and move freely.

statement: Water expands when it freezes because freezing makes its particles gain energy and move faster.
explanation: False! Water loses energy as it freezes. Its particles form an open arrangement that takes up more space; they do not gain energy.

statement: A puddle cannot dry on a 28°C day because water only changes into gas at 100°C.
explanation: False! Evaporation occurs at the surface below the boiling point, so the puddle can dry without boiling.

statement: Water drops can form outside a cold sealed bottle even if no liquid leaks out.
explanation: True! Water vapour in the surrounding air cools and condenses on the cold surface.

statement: The visible white cloud above a kettle proves that water vapour gas is white.
explanation: False! Water vapour gas is invisible. The visible cloud consists mainly of tiny liquid droplets formed by condensation.

statement: Equal volumes of water at the same temperature usually evaporate faster from a wide shallow tray than from a narrow cup under the same airflow.
explanation: True! The tray exposes more surface area, allowing more particles to escape per second.

statement: Condensation occurs because water vapour gains energy and its particles move farther apart.
explanation: False! During condensation, water vapour loses thermal energy and its particles come closer together to form liquid.

statement: Cloud formation and rain involve different processes: condensation forms droplets, while precipitation brings water down to Earth.
explanation: True! Condensation changes gas to liquid. Precipitation is water falling from clouds as rain, snow or hail.

statement: Once rain reaches the ocean, it cannot take part in the water cycle again.
explanation: False! Ocean water can evaporate, later condense into clouds and return as precipitation. The cycle continues.

statement: Rainwater that soaks into soil can still take part in the water cycle.
explanation: True! It may become groundwater, move towards rivers or be absorbed by plants and later released through transpiration.

statement: Salt has stopped existing when it can no longer be seen in a clear salt solution.
explanation: False! Salt particles are still present, spread throughout the water. Evaporating the water can recover the salt.

statement: In sugar water, sugar is the solute and water is the solvent.
explanation: True! Sugar is the substance dissolved, and water is the liquid that dissolves it.

statement: Ordinary filter paper can recover dissolved salt from salt water just as it separates sand from water.
explanation: False! Dissolved salt passes through ordinary filter paper with the water. Evaporation can recover the salt.

statement: A clear solution can contain a coloured dissolved substance.
explanation: True! Clear means transparent, not necessarily colourless. A coloured solution can still be uniform and transparent.

statement: Water being called the universal solvent means that sand and plastic must dissolve in it.
explanation: False! Water dissolves many substances, but not all. Sand and ordinary plastic do not dissolve in water.

statement: Evaporating all the water from a salt solution can recover solid salt, showing that this dissolving process is reversible.
explanation: True! The salt remains after the solvent leaves as water vapour. Reversibility means the starting substances can be recovered.

statement: A student can fairly test the effect of water temperature on dissolving time by using more sugar in the hotter water.
explanation: False! Changing both temperature and sugar amount makes the result ambiguous. The sugar amount must stay the same.

statement: When only stirring speed is changed, the time taken for salt to dissolve can be the dependent variable.
explanation: True! Stirring speed is deliberately changed; dissolving time is measured. Other relevant factors should stay the same.

statement: If sugar dissolves faster in warm water, this result alone proves that a larger maximum amount can dissolve there.
explanation: False! Dissolving time measures speed, not the maximum amount that can dissolve. A separate investigation is needed.

statement: River water is safe for wildlife whenever dissolved factory waste cannot be seen.
explanation: False! Harmful substances can dissolve and remain invisible in a solution. Appearance alone cannot establish safety.
